conditions: x is finite real and ln is the strictly real logarithm. Determine the complete real domain from the original operations.
Require an explicit exact antiderivative on the whole connected original domain, up to one additive constant. An unevaluated integral or numerical quadrature is not acceptable.

properties: The exact original domain is (0,infinity). Return the displayed primitive or an equivalent explicit exact primitive with this domain.
The displayed normalization has F(1)=-2, F'(1)=0, and limit zero as x tends to positive infinity.
The integrand and primitive are regular at x=1. No division by ln(x) may create an artificial hole there.
The exact improper integral from 1 to positive infinity is 2. Neither negative x nor x=0 belongs to the original real domain.

cases.reason: The original ln(x) requires x>0, which also ensures the denominator x^2 is nonzero; these conditions are necessary and sufficient. Write L=ln(x). Integration by parts with u=L^2 and dv=dx/x^2 gives I=-L^2/x+2*integrate(L/x^2,x). A second integration by parts gives integrate(L/x^2,x)=-L/x-1/x, hence F=-(L^2+2*L+2)/x. Direct differentiation yields F'=[L^2+2*L+2-(2*L+2)]/x^2=L^2/x^2 throughout x>0. Substitution at 1 gives the exact value and derivative. For the limit at infinity put x=exp(t); then F=-(t^2+2*t+2)*exp(-t), which tends to zero because exponential growth dominates a quadratic polynomial. The fundamental theorem on [1,b] followed by b tending to infinity proves the convergent improper integral equals 0-(-2)=2.

conditions: x is finite real and angles are in radians. Determine the complete real domain of the integrand independently of the integration interval.
This is the definite integral over [0,pi], including both endpoints. Require an explicit exact value; an unevaluated integral or numerical approximation is not acceptable.

properties: The complete real domain of the integrand is R, because 1+cos(x)^2>=1. The integrand is smooth everywhere.
Both endpoints of the integration interval are ordinary regular points with integrand value zero. No improper-integral convention is needed.
The exact integral is pi^2/4. Reflection x to pi-x provides an exact evaluation without requiring an elementary indefinite primitive for the weighted integrand.
The associated unweighted integral of sin(x)/(1+cos(x)^2) over [0,pi] is pi/2.

cases.reason: The real sine and cosine exist for every real x and the denominator is at least 1, proving the full original domain R and endpoint regularity. Set g(x)=sin(x)/(1+cos(x)^2). Since sin(pi-x)=sin(x) and cos(pi-x)=-cos(x), g(pi-x)=g(x). Substituting u=pi-x into I=integrate(x*g(x),x,0,pi) therefore gives I=integrate((pi-u)*g(u),u,0,pi). Adding the two equal representations yields 2*I=pi*integrate(g(x),x,0,pi). In the remaining integral t=cos(x), dt=-sin(x) dx, and the endpoints become 1 and -1, so its value is integrate(1/(1+t^2),t,-1,1)=atan(1)-atan(-1)=pi/2. Thus 2*I=pi^2/2 and I=pi^2/4. Every substitution is on a compact interval with a continuous integrand.

conditions: x is finite real. piecewise selects its first true branch lazily, so the exponential branch is evaluated only for x>0.
Determine the ordinary two-sided derivative on the complete original domain. In particular, compute the original difference quotient at x=0 using its assigned value f(0)=0.
No extension is requested: the original piecewise function already defines every real x.

properties: The complete original domain and the exact ordinary derivative domain are both R. The derivative at zero is exactly zero.
The derivative is zero for x<=0 and strictly positive for x>0. It is continuous at zero.
The original function is infinitely differentiable at zero and every derivative there is zero, although the function is positive for every positive x.
At x=1 the exact derivative is exp(-1). A result that evaluates 1/x in an inactive branch or declares zero undefined is incorrect.

cases.reason: For x<=0 the selected branch is the constant zero. For x>0 the reciprocal and exponential are defined, so lazy branch selection gives exactly the whole real line as the original domain. On the positive open half-line the chain rule gives exp(-1/x)/x^2, and on the negative open half-line the derivative is zero. At zero, the original quotient is zero for h<0; for h>0 it is exp(-1/h)/h=t*exp(-t), where t=1/h tends to positive infinity. The exponential series gives exp(t)>=t^3/6, so 0<=t*exp(-t)<=6/t^2, proving the actual two-sided derivative is zero. Similarly the positive-side derivative is t^2*exp(-t), which tends to zero, proving continuity at the join. More generally every positive-side derivative has the form P_n(1/x)*exp(-1/x) with a polynomial P_n: differentiation changes P_n(t) to t^2*(P_n(t)-P_n'(t)). Every such polynomial times exp(-t), and its product with t for the next difference quotient, tends to zero. Induction using the already assigned zero values on x<=0 proves all derivatives at zero exist and vanish. This argument never evaluates the inactive reciprocal at zero.

conditions: x is finite real and floor(x) is the greatest integer not exceeding x, including for negative x.
The original function is defined on all of R. Determine its actual ordinary derivative at every integer as well as between integers.
At each integer use the original two-sided difference quotient with the original value. The nondifferentiability of floor by itself does not settle differentiability of the whole function.

properties: The exact derivative domain is all of R. At every integer n, the original value f(n) and the derivative f'(n) are both zero.
The displayed derivative is globally valid and directly evaluates to zero at each integer without an additional limiting convention.
The function and its derivative have period 1. On each interval (n,n+1/2) the derivative is positive, and on (n+1/2,n+1) it is negative.
At every half-integer n+1/2 the function is 1/16 and its derivative is zero. The function is twice continuously differentiable but is not three times differentiable at any integer.
No integer, including any negative integer, may become an artificial derivative-domain hole.

cases.reason: Write t=x-floor(x), so 0<=t<1 for every real x, and f=t^2*(1-t)^2. On (n,n+1), floor(x)=n is constant and ordinary polynomial differentiation yields f'=2*t*(1-t)*(1-2*t). At an integer n the original value is zero. For 0<h<1, f(n+h)=h^2*(1-h)^2, giving quotient h*(1-h)^2. For -1<h<0, floor(n+h)=n-1 and f(n+h)=(1+h)^2*h^2, giving quotient h*(1+h)^2. Both quotients tend to zero, which equals the displayed formula at t=0. The derivative polynomial tends to zero at both t=0 and t=1, so the derivative is continuous at every integer. Between integers f''=2-12*t+12*t^2; its two limiting values at each integer are both 2. The one-sided difference quotients of f' at n also both tend to 2, proving f''(n)=2 and global continuity of f''. The right derivative of f'' at n is -12 while its left derivative is 12, so f'''(n) does not exist. Periodicity follows from floor(x+1)=floor(x)+1, and signs and half-integer values follow by substitution into the polynomial formulas. All joining calculations apply to arbitrary integers n, with no restriction on their sign.

conditions: x and y are finite real numbers and all angles are in radians. Each original tangent and each original quotient must be defined.
Determine and retain the complete original real domain. Return zero together with that domain, or an equivalent exact guarded expression; unrestricted zero is not acceptable.
piecewise selects its first true branch lazily. This case generalizes the recent cancelled-factor domain-loss failure to a two-variable trigonometric identity with infinitely many excluded lines.

properties: The exact original domain is cos(x)!=0 and cos(y)!=0 and cos(x+y)!=0. The value is identically zero on exactly this domain.
The excluded set consists of x=pi/2+k*pi, y=pi/2+k*pi, or x+y=pi/2+k*pi for any integer k. All these lines must remain excluded.
In particular (pi/2,pi/2) is excluded even though tan(x+y) alone is defined there, and (pi/4,pi/4) is excluded even though each of tan(x) and tan(y) is defined there.
The points (0,0), (pi/4,-pi/4), and (pi,pi) are allowed and have value zero. The domain and value are unchanged by adding an integer multiple of pi to either variable.
Exact retention of an equivalent domain-bearing trigonometric expression is acceptable; cancellation must not silently supply values on excluded lines.

cases.reason: The first two original tangents require cos(x) and cos(y) to be nonzero, and the last requires cos(x+y) nonzero. Under the first two conditions, 1-tan(x)*tan(y)=[cos(x)*cos(y)-sin(x)*sin(y)]/[cos(x)*cos(y)]=cos(x+y)/[cos(x)*cos(y)]. Thus nonvanishing of the original quotient denominator is exactly the third condition, and there are no other restrictions. Likewise tan(x)+tan(y)=sin(x+y)/[cos(x)*cos(y)]. Division, valid only under all three conditions, gives the first quotient equal to tan(x+y), so the difference is zero. The real zeros of cosine establish the stated complete excluded lines. At (pi/2,pi/2) the first two tangents are undefined although cos(x+y)=-1; at (pi/4,pi/4) the original quotient denominator and cos(x+y) both vanish. Exact substitution verifies the three allowed examples. Shifting either variable by an integer multiple of pi preserves nonvanishing of all three cosines and preserves tangent values. This proves a domain-qualified identity and does not define a continuation across any excluded line.

conditions: x is finite real. The original sum has exactly 21 terms, k=0 through 20; the degree and bounds are fixed numeric constants.

Each invocation has a fixed 10-second external wall-clock timeout and a 65536-byte output cap. Preserve all existing configured finite CG50 stack, heap and simplification budgets; do not enlarge limits or retry with enlarged limits.
Exact retention of the original compact finite sum, or an equivalent compact exact representation, is acceptable. Expansion of each twentieth power is not required.

properties: The complete original domain is R. The sum is the constant 20!=2432902008176640000 for every real x.
Return this exact integer, an equivalent exact expression such as factorial(20), or retain the original compact finite sum exactly.
No cancellation may introduce a domain exclusion; in particular x=0, x=-10 and every x=-k occurring in a summand are ordinary allowed points.
No floating-point replacement is acceptable. Individual terms may be large and alternate in sign, but the exact answer is the same positive integer for every x.
No crash, stack overflow, timeout, output-cap overrun, runaway expansion or undef at an allowed point is acceptable. Resource limits must not be increased.
Compact exact retention is a resource-case alternative and does not relax the explicit exact-answer requirements for either integral.

cases.reason: Every summand is a polynomial in x multiplied by fixed integers, proving the original domain is all R with no exceptional zeros or poles. Define the forward difference of a polynomial by Delta p(x)=p(x+1)-p(x). Induction on n using Pascal's binomial identity gives Delta^n p(x)=sum((-1)^(n-k)*binomial(n,k)*p(x+k),k,0,n). For a polynomial with degree m>=1 and leading coefficient a, the binomial theorem shows Delta p has degree m-1 and leading coefficient a*m. Starting with p(x)=x^20, applying Delta twenty times therefore yields the constant 20*19*...*1=20!. Since 20 is even, (-1)^(20-k)=(-1)^k, so the displayed original sum is precisely Delta^20 p(x). Exact integer multiplication gives 20!=2432902008176640000. The finite-difference proof establishes the identity on every real x without evaluating or expanding all 21 powers and without division by any expression involving x.
